findings.claim: Key Fact: "Three UK laws you must know: Data Protection Act 2018 ... Computer Misuse Act 1990 ... Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988".
findings.truth: Section 3.8 of the spec names no legislation at all. Its examinable list is cyber security, mobile technologies, wireless networking, cloud storage, hacking, wearable technologies, computer based implants and autonomous vehicles, and it states that students need the general principles rather than detailed knowledge of specific issues. The Acts are useful context, not required content, so "must know" overstates the spec.
findings.evidence: spec 3.8 content and additional-information columns (spec lines 2010-2050)

findings.claim: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 "covers three categories of offence: ... and unauthorised modification of computer material" (repeated in the <dfn> data-def and in glossary_terms).
findings.truth: Section 3 of the Act was substituted by the Police and Justice Act 2006 and now reads "Unauthorised acts with intent to impair, or with recklessness as to impairing, operation of computer, etc." The 1990 wording "unauthorised modification of computer material" is repealed. The Act as amended also carries s.3ZA and s.3A, so "three categories" needs "main".
findings.evidence: legislation.gov.uk, Computer Misuse Act 1990 s.3 (substituted 1 Oct 2007 Scotland / 1 Oct 2008 elsewhere by the Police and Justice Act 2006)

findings.claim: "A 2015 amendment to the Act increased maximum penalties and added offences relating to attacks on computer infrastructure."
findings.truth: The Serious Crime Act 2015 inserted s.3ZA (unauthorised acts causing, or creating risk of, serious damage), carrying up to 14 years, or life where human welfare or national security is harmed. It did not raise the maximum penalty for the existing offences; the s.1 maximum rose from six months to two years under the Police and Justice Act 2006.
findings.evidence: Serious Crime Act 2015 s.41 inserting CMA s.3ZA; Police and Justice Act 2006 penalty change (legislation.gov.uk; Wikipedia, Computer Misuse Act 1990)

findings.claim: "For 4-mark or 8-mark questions on ethical or legal issues, examiners reward balance and specificity."
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim, and it asserts tariffs the spec does not set. The spec states only that Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes, 90 marks, 50% of the GCSE, drawn from 3.3-3.8, with multiple-choice, short-answer, longer-answer and extended-response questions. Say what a good answer contains without speaking for examiners.

findings.claim: "a clear descriptive explanation of what each law prohibits earns full marks without invented detail."
findings.truth: A mark-scheme promise we cannot make. No AQA mark scheme awards full marks for describing a law, and 3.8 sets no legislation content. Describe what the answer needs instead of promising marks.
findings.evidence: spec 3.8; house rule on board mark-scheme claims

findings.claim: "Producing electronic devices requires mining rare earth minerals and metals including lithium, cobalt, gold and tantalum."
findings.truth: None of lithium, cobalt, gold or tantalum is a rare earth element. The rare earths are the fifteen lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium, for example neodymium and dysprosium. Lithium is an alkali metal; cobalt, gold and tantalum are transition metals. The sentence teaches a wrong definition of a technical term.
findings.evidence: standard chemistry definition of the rare earth elements (lanthanides plus Sc and Y)

findings.claim: Question 6, "State two ways that individuals can help reduce the environmental impact of their electronic devices", is labelled "2 marks — State a Difference".
findings.truth: The question asks for two separate methods, not a difference between two things. The house label for this format is "2 marks — State Two". The wrong label tells the student to write a comparison, which would not answer the question.
findings.evidence: question stem against the house question-type vocabulary used across the corpus

findings.claim: "Current legal frameworks are not well-equipped to deal with this complexity" (content_html), echoed by the flashcard answer "legal frameworks assume a human driver".
findings.truth: Dated for the UK. The Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018 already makes the insurer primarily liable when an automated vehicle is driving itself, and the Automated Vehicles Act 2024 (Royal Assent 20 May 2024) creates an authorisation and in-use regulation regime with a named responsible entity. Options: (a) leave as is, because the spec asks only for general principles and naming statutes exceeds the required depth; (b) soften to "the law is still catching up" without naming an Act; (c) name the Automated Vehicles Act 2024 in one clause. Option (c) adds content the spec does not need and two more facts to maintain.
findings.evidence: Automated Vehicles Act 2024; Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018; spec 3.8 "general principles behind the issues rather than ... detailed knowledge"
findings.ruling: NOTE: 'legal frameworks not yet well-equipped' is dated (AEVA 2018, Automated Vehicles Act 2024) but the spec wants general principles; left.

summary: Both lessons are sound on the spec's own ground; the errors sit in the legislation detail the spec never asked for. The fixes correct the repealed Computer Misuse Act section 3 wording, the misattributed 2015 amendment, two fabricated examiner and mark-scheme claims, a "rare earth" mislabel and one wrong practice-question type. Every knowledge-check key and match order in both lessons recomputed correct.
